oneliner.t: Democratic former U.S. senator (2007–2025) and congressman from Ohio, three-term Senate Banking Committee leader who lost his seat to Bernie Moreno in 2024, now the Democratic nominee in the 2026 special election against appointed Sen. Jon Husted.

upbringing.t: Brown was born and raised in Mansfield, Ohio. His mother was Emily Campbell Brown and his father, Charles Gailey Brown, was a physician. He became an Eagle Scout in 1967 and graduated from Mansfield Senior High School in 1970. He earned a B.A. in Russian studies at Yale in 1974, the same year he was elected to the Ohio House. He later earned an M.A. in education (1979) and an M.P.A. (1981) at Ohio State and taught at its Mansfield branch campus. He is married to Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist Connie Schultz.

career.role: Ohio Secretary of State (lost 1990 reelection to Bob Taft)
U.S. Senator; Banking Committee ranking member 2015–2021, chair 2021–2025

platform.t: Lists affordability and health-care cost reform as his core issue: take on insurers, lower prescription prices for seniors, and cap seniors' insulin costs at $35.
Restore pensions for retirees he says were 'fleeced by Wall Street' and restore Social Security benefits for Ohio workers.

Opposes large tax breaks for billionaires and corporations. He says he re-entered politics because of the 2025 tax-and-spending law, which he calls a 'rigged system' that cut programs such as Medicaid.
Runs on a pro-worker, pro-union agenda and attacks tariffs for raising prices. He opposed NAFTA and later backed USMCA as a step toward pro-worker trade.

Calls for ending Ohio's data-center tax break, limiting data centers' water use and keeping their electricity costs off consumers' bills; says Ohioans should decide whether data centers are built in their communities.
As Banking chair he called for comprehensive crypto legislation after the FTX collapse. He says crypto should expand opportunity without putting Ohioans at risk.

promises.t: Cap seniors' out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 and lower prescription-drug prices.
Restore pensions for retirees and Social Security benefits for Ohio workers.
End Ohio's data-center tax break and keep data centers' power costs off household bills.
Fight tax breaks for the wealthy and cuts to programs like Medicaid.

claims.claim: Youngest person elected to the Ohio House, in 1974.

record.t: He was elected in 1974, the year he finished Yale, at about age 21–22. No Ohio House record confirming 'youngest ever' was opened.

claims.claim: Served as Ohio Secretary of State and lost a second-term bid in 1990 to Bob Taft.

record.t: He was Secretary of State 1983–1991. He was elected in 1982, reelected in 1986, and lost the 1990 race to Bob Taft, so that was a bid for a third term, not a second. WFMJ's summary describes it both ways.

claims.claim: Represented Ohio's 13th District for seven terms.

record.t: U.S. House, OH-13, 1993–2007: seven two-year terms.

claims.claim: Won his Senate seat in 2006 and served 18 years.

said.where: campaign biography as summarized by WFMJ

record.t: Defeated Mike DeWine in 2006 and served Jan. 3, 2007–Jan. 3, 2025.
Wikipedia records a 1992 move to Lorain and later Cleveland property. No current voter or property record was opened.

claims.claim: Has 'always overperformed his party,' getting more than 100,000 more votes than Kamala Harris in Ohio in 2024.

record.t: He lost by 3.6 points while Trump carried Ohio by about 11, and NOTUS reports he received over 100,000 more votes than Harris. Official county returns were not opened.

claims.claim: Husted is 'the face of data centers in Ohio' who 'cut sweetheart tax deals' and fast-tracked approvals while electric bills rose.

said.where: Brown TV ad (July 2026), the campaign's most-covered ad

record.t: Husted championed data-center growth as lieutenant governor, and Ohio's data-center tax break cost $1.6 billion last year against a $135 million state estimate. No specific tax deal personally negotiated by Husted, or approval he fast-tracked, is documented in the sources opened. Republicans note that Brown backed a Columbus-area data center in 2015.

claims.claim: 'Nobody in the Senate is speaking out for Ohio workers, nobody.'

record.t: A characterization, not a checkable fact.

claims.claim: Husted's career 'has been about special interests,' citing his ties to the utility at the center of the HB 6 bribery scheme.

record.t: The documented ties: Husted attended a 2018 dinner with FirstEnergy executives later indicted; FirstEnergy gave $1M earmarked 'Husted campaign' to Freedom Frontier in 2017, which his campaign says it never received; and he testified as a defense witness in 2026. He has never been charged. The 'special interests' framing is opinion.

said.t: Long-time critic of free-trade deals he says send Ohio jobs abroad.

did.t: Voted against NAFTA as a congressman and later supported its replacement, USMCA, as a step toward pro-worker trade.

said.t: Calls for ending Ohio's data-center tax break and says communities should decide whether data centers are built.

did.t: Republicans point out that he supported a Columbus-area data center project in 2015. Google's PAC gave his committee $20,000 over his career, and Google lobbyists gave several thousand dollars more. These are donations, not votes, and no documented link to a position was found.

entries.t: Signed an AIPAC-backed letter urging President Obama to veto 'one-sided' UN resolutions against Israel.
Voted against the Israel anti-boycott (anti-BDS) legislation.
Urged recognition of a 'nonmilitarized' Palestinian state.
Attacks Trump's tariffs for raising prices.

aipac_endorse.t: Not listed. AIPAC's 2026 Ohio Senate endorsement went to Husted. Brown is endorsed by the Jewish Democratic Council of America.

note.t: Not a sitting member; no current disclosure was opened. In 2023 NBC reported late Cleveland property-tax payments and owner-occupant credits claimed in two counties. He repaid Franklin County and said he would stop claiming the credit. The same year he corrected several years of Senate financial disclosures that had omitted his wife's pension income.

democracy.t: As a House member, voted Nay on the objection to Ohio's 2004 electoral votes (accepting the certified result).
Voted Nay on the Senate objections to Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electoral votes.

access.debates_note: As of Aug. 7, 2026 no debate had been agreed to. Brown said, 'I assume we are,' and that he had debated in most campaigns, but he had not accepted a specific debate. In 2024 he and Moreno did not debate, and each side blamed the other.

note.t: Born in Mansfield in 1952. He left Ohio for Yale (1970–74), returned, and won the Ohio House seat in 1974. He has lived in Ohio since, apart from Washington service; he moved to Lorain in 1992. The years figure excludes college.

checks.legal: No direct court searches: CourtListener and Justia URLs could not be fetched in this environment, so courts is 'news'. Wikipedia reports that during his 1986–87 divorce his then-wife obtained a restraining order and alleged violence and intimidation in an affidavit. She later walked back the claims and hosted a 2012 fundraiser for him. No charges were found. Senate Ethics Committee pages were not searched.

corp.t: Career: $4,768,563 from corporate PACs and $1,872,665 from trade-association PACs (FEC records, 2000–2026). The 2026 cycle is much smaller: $27,843 corporate and $2,500 trade. Google's PAC gave $20,000 over his career.

lobby.t: Career money from committees organized around Israel policy: J Street PAC $145,916, JACPAC $38,008, FIPAC $10,000, World Alliance for Israel PAC $3,000 and NORPAC $1,000, plus $33,400 bundled by J Street in 2026. Small sums came from committees named for other countries: Taiwanese American PACs $8,000, ARMENPAC $2,000, Arab American Leadership Council PAC $2,000, Irish American Democrats $1,000 and Americans for a Palestinian State $400.

research_notes: MONEY: 2026 totals through 2026-06-30 are from the records pull of FEC data. Individuals gave $31,146,133, committees $861,023 and party $200; the 'other' $6,558,878 is mainly transfers from joint-fundraising committees with the Ohio Democratic Party and DSCC. The itemized/unitemized split wasn't available. Legis1 reports more than 100,000 Q1 2026 donors averaging about $35 and roughly 43% of itemized money from Ohio, but that share is not computed here. The records' 2026 PAC classification sums to only $232,830 against the $861,023 'other committees' line, so pac_biz/pac_ideo are omitted. Cycle history pairs two FEC IDs per cycle: the main committee row is used, and small leftover rows from a second committee are omitted (2000: $31,530; 2002: $41,100; 2004: $29,525; 2006: $545). Outside spending is from FEC Schedule E records as of 2026-10-13, top 10 spenders only. UDP is not among them, so its figure is null. The $54.0M from SLF PAC is the largest single item. RESIDENCE: WFMJ says he lives in Columbus, while Wikipedia mentions Lorain and Cleveland, so this needs a human check. Wikipedia's Ohio House dates conflict (1975–1983 in the infobox, 1974–1982 in the text). Not rated: the 1986–87 divorce affidavit, recanted and never charged, which is noted under checks.legal for editorial decision rather than listed as a legal finding.
